extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, math-rubric designers, and anyone evaluating mathematical theories or research
extracted.subtask_description: Provide a multi-axis evaluation of a mathematical theory or piece of mathematical work using Kuhn's five adapted criteria (accuracy, consistency, scope, simplicity, fruitfulness), plus meta-guidance about weighting and framework-dependence. Useful for peer review, curriculum design, and methodological reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy / correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement with observed data; in mathematics, agreement with prior theorems and accepted results. Does it follow from accepted axioms / prior results without error?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score the work on rigorous correctness: proofs must follow from accepted axioms/prior results without error. In the rubric-adaptation: 'Accuracy / correctness: Does it follow from accepted axioms / prior results without error?' Also consider whether established results survive within a new framework when evaluating paradigm shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal logical consistency, and consistency with other accepted theories. Is it internally consistent and consistent with the rest of mathematics?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both internal coherence of definitions/arguments and external coherence with established mathematics. Check for contradictions with accepted theorems or foundational frameworks. For paradigm shifts, ask whether the new framework is consistent with established mathematics (or how it reconciles differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent of consequences beyond the data the theory was built to explain. Does it apply to many cases, or just one?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how broadly the results apply: many cases or isolated instances. Scope maps onto generality in mathematics; greater scope means the theory/theorem has wider applicability or explanatory reach across subareas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to organize phenomena that would otherwise be confused or isolated. Does it organize previously isolated phenomena under one principle?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret simplicity in terms of organizing power or elegance: does the approach reduce complexity, unify disparate results, or lower ontological/mathematical commitments? Note ambiguity in what counts as 'simplicity' (ontological vs. formal simplicity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity for further research; opening of new questions. Does it open new problems, suggest new methods, generate further work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure generativity: does the work suggest new directions, conjectures, tools, or connections that lead to additional mathematics? Fruitfulness includes whether the framework produces new theorems or research programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping to mathematical virtues (rigor, coherence, generality, elegance, generativity)
rubrics_metrics.description: These five axes map roughly onto 'rigor, coherence, generality, elegance, and generativity' and provide a five-axis rubric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When communicating scores, it can be helpful to translate Kuhn's terminology into mathematicians' language (e.g., accuracy→rigor, consistency→coherence). This mapping aids readability but does not change the underlying criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria underdetermine choice (Kuhn's caveat)
rubrics_metrics.description: The five criteria do not uniquely determine theory choice: which features satisfy each criterion is disputable; the criteria are imprecise; the criteria can conflict; different scientists weight them differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect a single algorithmic verdict. Reasonable people can disagree about how well a theory scores on each axis. Use the rubric to make disagreements explicit (locate them on axes) rather than to force consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring practice: multi-axis independent scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Score independently on each axis; do not collapse to a single quality number; acknowledge that ranking is partly community-relative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rubrics to record independent scores for accuracy, consistency, scope, simplicity, and fruitfulness. Use the multi-axis profile for comparison and to reveal trade-offs. Explicitly note weights or community-relative preferences if a comparative ordering is required, but avoid presenting a sole aggregated score as authoritative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framework-dependence and incommensurability
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that mathematicians working in different foundational frameworks may legitimately disagree about what counts as a theorem or an acceptable method; competing paradigms can be incommensurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating work, ask whether it requires a specific paradigm; if so, evaluate it within that paradigm before comparing across frameworks. A rubric must allow for framework-relative judgments and acknowledge that some disagreements reflect incommensurability rather than evaluative error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm-shift evaluation checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions to evaluate a proposed paradigm shift: Does it give simpler proofs of established theorems? Does it have wider scope? Is it consistent with established mathematics? Is it fruitful (produces new theorems, opens new problems)? Is it accurate (do established results survive in the new framework)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five targeted questions when assessing proposed foundational or methodological shifts. They mirror the main axes but are framed as specific tests for paradigm-level change; document how the new paradigm performs on each to track controversies and eventual acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of rubric: no algorithmic verdicts and role of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: A rubric cannot deliver algorithmic verdicts; it cannot combine the axes into a single ranking that all reasonable judges should accept; it cannot eliminate the role of taste or resolve framework-level disagreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat limits as features: make trade-offs visible, use the rubric to structure productive disagreement, and accept that some evaluation aspects remain partly subjective or community-dependent. Avoid overreliance on numerical aggregation.
